articles.text: Calif. tops 1 million reported cases; Piedmont total now 57 Due to an ongoing spike in COVID-19 cases for more than two weeks, Alameda County enacted purple tier restrictions for business and activities starting today, Wednesday, November 18. The state placed the entire county, which includes Piedmont, into the purple tier, a more restrictive category, on Monday, November 16. The purple tier is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system. The state moved Alameda County into the second-least restrictive orange tier, or moderate tier, on October 13. This week, the county skipped the red tier, or substantial tier, and was moved directly into the most restrictive category. The California Department of Public Health said that local and statewide increases in new cases caused the change in tier. According to the state, counties are placed in the purple tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. “We need Alameda County residents and businesses to, once again, rise to the challenge and help flatten the curve,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Health Officer, in a statement. Four more cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont during the past seven days, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department released yesterday, Tuesday, November 17. The total caseload for Piedmont since the pandemic began in March is now 57. New cases have been rising steadily in recent days in Alameda County. On Monday, 206 new cases were reported, compared to 35 reported on October 15. On August 13, the worst day yet for the county, 419 cases were recorded. articles.text: City hopes to replace retaining walls on San Carlos Ave. On Monday, November 16, City Council directed the Public Works Department to come up with a plan to replace retaining walls on San Carlos Avenue and a portion of Oakland Ave. near Sunnyside, both of which are deteriorating and leaning. The City hopes to complete the work by next spring, 2021. “This is a long-time public project that we’ve been working on,” noted Director of Public Works Chester Nakahara, who retires in December. He added that the project had been derailed by the coronavirus pandemic this year. The leaning wall on Oakland Avenue runs between Sunnyside and Olive Avenues. The wall on San Carlos Avenue runs on the lower roadway of that split-level street. Both walls have large cracks and are leaning significantly. If the retaining walls were to fail, it would impact the sidewalks, roadways and potentially private property. “These walls are aging, and have been leaning outwards towards the street,” Nakahara wrote in a staff report. The walls were initially cast in place, where concrete is poured to create the wall at the site. The council agreed with City staff’s recommendation that the new walls be created in this “castin-place” method, which could match the existing appearance of the walls as well as allow for some ornamentation. In replacing the existing retaining walls this way, the City could create an Oakland Avenue “bioswale,” a planted channel that removes water pollution. Other options presented to Council by civil engineer John Wanger included the “big blocks” method, where pre-cast blocks are stacked to create a new wall, and the tie-back “shotcrete” method where a natural-looking concrete wall is fastened to some of the existing wall and adjacent soil. Council also considered the “concrete masonry unit” method, where a new wall is built in front of the old and would require relocating the sidewalk, gutter and curb. articles.text: State measure passes with 56% majority Alastair Mactaggart A Piedmont couple, Celine and Alastair Mactaggart, can be credited with sponsoring the California Privacy Rights Act, seen on this year’s ballot as Proposition 24. The latest count shows that Prop. 24 is passing with a majority of 56 percent. The Privacy Rights Act will reinforce and redefine parts of the California Consumer Privacy Act, a 2019 law that gave state residents new rights as to how companies collect and use their personal information. Supporters of the proposition say that the new law will make it easier for people to opt out of having their 24 has as a central provision that no future amendments that harm consumer privacy would be permitted. Any other amendments, for example to help consumer privacy, are permitted with a simple majority vote of the Legislature, but anything that harmed consumer privacy would require another initiative.” This would eliminate the efforts of special interest groups in the legislature who may try to weaken the law. “Nearly one million voters signed a petition to put Proposition 24 on the ballot,” she added. The new law is designed to place power back into the hands of consumers. “I’ve worked very hard on this issue for six years, and we actually think privacy is the wrong word. This is really about power. Large companies buy and sell our personal information and data over and over again, every day without our knowledge or consent,” she explained. “Prop. 24 puts strong guardrails on that, so this is really about giving people a choice about their own personal information, like that of their race, ethnicity, or health, and letting them decide who gets to use it, or not.” The law will also triple fines for abuses of kids’ data. It will now require opt-in consent for the sale of personal information from consumers under the age of 16. “It will set a strong floor whereby future amendments to the law can only be made in furtherance of protecting privacy, creating a one-way switch for future protection,” Celine Mactaggart said. articles.text: Just after 4 a.m. EST on Friday, November 6, three days after America’s contentious presidential election, Georgia was not yet on everyone’s mind. Every major news network still colored the state with 16 electoral votes pink for a slight lead for Donald Trump. However, a local independent reporter, Robin Kemp from Georgia’s Clayton County, was able to break the news of Biden overtaking Trump in Georgia as it happened. The few hundred people following the updates on her Twitter account got the news first, while the rest of country sat in the dark. The now famous reporter, Robin Kemp, recently set up the first nonprofit news site in Clayton County, Georgia. She created The Clayton Crescent after the local county paper laid her off due to COVID-19. Even without a paycheck, Kemp kept reporting election results as they trickled in. She arrived at the Registrar’s office in Clayton County at 9:00 a.m. Thursday and didn’t leave until 5:09 a.m. Friday when the count was finished. As the vote tallies in Georgia came down to the end, Clayton County still had a few thousand mail-in ballots and the county just south of Atlanta hit the global spotlight. After 3:00 a.m. Friday, November 6, at least one major news network mistakenly announced Georgia’s Clayton County (which was voting 87 percent for Biden) had stopped counting and reporting numbers for the night. Kemp, originally from New Orleans, has been a reporter in Georgia for some years. She describes herself as “A spicy Popeyes sandwich out here Local, independent journalist Robin Kemp covered the breaking news ahead of the major networks, as Georgia flipped to blue in the presidential election on November 3 for the first time since 1992. in a Chick-Fil-A world.” Her dedicated exclusive coverage included interviews with GOP observers, and photos in the Registrar’s office of ballots being delivered, verified for signatures, stacked, counted and zip tied when done. She fielded questions from anxious followers on her Twitter and gave live video updates with the latest number of ballots outstanding, happenings in the office and presidential votes. Some news crews rushed to the Registrar’s office towards the end of Friday night, but Kemp was the only one there the entire day. Kemp gave the world updates from the ground and referred people to the county website to see that Biden had taken the lead by 917 votes just after 4 a.m. of Friday. She found herself suddenly with a touch of fame, being interviewed by reporters as far away as England. Someone dredged up an old GoFundMe for www. claytoncrescent.com and her new “Sleeping here at night is OK, but not walking around my carpet in your golf shoes.”

Privacy Rights Act sponsored by Piedmont couple State measure passes with 56% majority By Allyson Aleksey A Piedmont couple, Celine and Alastair Mactaggart, can be credited with sponsoring the California Privacy Rights Act, seen on this year’s ballot as Proposition 24. The latest count shows that Prop. 24 is passing with a majority of 56 percent. The Privacy Rights Act will reinforce and redefine parts of the California Consumer Privacy Act, a 2019 law that gave state residents new rights as to how companies collect and use their personal information. Supporters of the proposition say that the new law will make it easier for people to opt out of having their data collected online. 24 has as a central provision that no future amendments that harm consumer privacy would be permitted. Any other amendments, for example to help consumer privacy, are permitted with a simple majority vote of the Legislature, but anything that harmed consumer privacy would require another initiative.” This would eliminate the efforts of special interest groups in the legislature who may try to weaken the law. “Nearly one million voters signed a petition to put Proposition 24 on the ballot,” she added. The new law is designed to place power back into the hands of consumers. “I’ve worked very hard on this issue for six years, and we actually think privacy is the wrong word. This is really about power. Large companies buy and sell our personal information and data over and over again, every day without our knowledge or consent,” she explained. “Prop. 24 puts strong guardrails on that, so this is really about giving people a choice about their own personal information, like that of their race, ethnicity, or health, and letting them decide who gets to use it, or not.” The law will also triple fines for abuses of kids’ data. It will now require opt-in consent for the sale of personal information from consumers under the age of 16. “It will set a strong floor whereby future amendments to the law can only be made in furtherance of protecting privacy, creating a one-way switch for future protection,” Celine Mactaggart said. The proposition was endorsed by many notable industry leaders in the state, including former presidential candidate Andrew Yang, Congressman Ro Khanna, privacy expert and author Shoshana Zuboff. Local journalist the star in Georgia election night coverage By Jay Russell Just after 4 a.m. EST on Friday, November 6, three days after America’s contentious presidential election, Georgia was not yet on everyone’s mind. Every major news network still colored the state with 16 electoral votes pink for a slight lead for Donald Trump. However, a local independent reporter, Robin Kemp from Georgia’s Clayton County, was able to break the news of Biden overtaking Trump in Georgia as it happened. The few hundred people following the updates on her Twitter account got the news first, while the rest of country sat in the dark. The now famous reporter, Robin Kemp, recently set up the first nonprofit news site in Clayton County, Georgia. She created The Clayton Crescent after the local county paper laid her off due to COVID-19. Even without a paycheck, Kemp kept reporting election results as they trickled in. She arrived at the Registrar’s office in Clayton County at 9:00 a.m. Thursday and didn’t leave until 5:09 a.m. Friday when the count was finished. As the vote tallies in Georgia came down to the end, Clayton County still had a few thousand mail-in ballots and the county just south of Atlanta hit the global spotlight. After 3:00 a.m. Friday, November 6, at least one major news network mistakenly announced Georgia’s Clayton County (which was voting 87 percent for Biden) had stopped counting and reporting numbers for the night. Kemp, originally from New Orleans, has been a reporter in Georgia for some years. She describes herself as “A spicy Popeyes sandwich out here Local, independent journalist Robin Kemp covered the breaking news ahead of the major networks, as Georgia flipped to blue in the presidential election on November 3 for the first time since 1992. in a Chick-Fil-A world.” Her dedicated exclusive coverage included interviews with GOP observers, and photos in the Registrar’s office of ballots being delivered, verified for signatures, stacked, counted and zip tied when done. She fielded questions from anxious followers on her Twitter and gave live video updates with the latest number of ballots outstanding, happenings in the office and presidential votes. Some news crews rushed to the Registrar’s office towards the end of Friday night, but Kemp was the only one there the entire day. Kemp gave the world updates from the ground and referred people to the county website to see that Biden had taken the lead by 917 votes just after 4 a.m. of Friday. She found herself suddenly with a touch of fame, being interviewed by reporters as far away as England. articles.text: The annual Toys for Tots campaign has begun, and Piedmont Fire Department has placed a donation box by the front doors of City Hall. Residents are encouraged to drop off new, unwrapped gifts for children in the bin during daytime hours seven days a week. Last year, the Marine Corps Reserve, which sponsors the nationwide campaign, had 109 donation sites in Alameda County and collected 25,000 toys to kids in the county. “With the help of Piedmont residents, we’re hoping that we can see that number go higher this year,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. articles.text: A current mural in progress by PCSC artists Ruby Guzdar (left), Cleopatra Tahawi, Quelam Tran Perez, Anabel Loucks, and Emma Jahn. With only three sheets of paper, eight pints of paint, and many helping hands, my design for the first tiny house mural came to life. Working alongside Piedmont High junior Anabel Loucks, senior Emma Jahn, and many other Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) members, I was able to create an art piece that captures Oakland’s rich culture and characteristic sense of collaboration. I was initially introduced to the mission of Youth Spirit Artworks (YSA) through the PCSC crew calendar, and I saw the tiny house mural project as an opportunity to utilize my passion for art and give back to my community. Loucks expressed a similar interest, “When I saw the mural design challenge, I loved the idea and threw myself into designing something that would inspire homeless teens [by] beautifying and changing the world around them,” she said. After finding out that both Loucks and Jahn had also submitted designs, I immediately asked them to help lead the project with me. While still under social distancing policies, we began by outlining my design onto the PCSC muralists Quelam Tran-Perez (left) and Emma Jahn. A finished mural on a tiny house.

articles.text: Trees are real – trees are sustainable Staff photo Oakland’s famous Tap Dancing Christmas Trees on opening day of the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot in 2018. Purchasing a real Christmas tree for the holidays is an environmentally friendly way to celebrate the season. Trees spend roughly eight years being grown before being harvested. They convert CO2 into oxygen, providing a habitat for wildlife and keeping large spaces of green across North America. Unlike artificial trees, they are 100% recyclable and 100% biodegradable. In our bold, new world, online sales are a lifeline for many; and during a time of COVID, the Piedmont Scout Council is taking a giant leap and offering tree sales online. For over 50 years, the Scouts have cheerfully procured, sold, trimmed and delivered everyone’s favorite conifers from Silver Tip to Noble and Douglas Firs. Online sale began November 1 and continue until all trees are sold, typically by about December 15. Sales are online at www. young participants. Last year the Scouts sold over 1,700 trees, raising $100,000 for Scout programs in Cub Scouts, Scouts, Explorers, Sea Scouts and coed Venturing programs. online sales and contactless pick-up and delivery, the Scouts allow customers to plan early for the Holidays, relaxing in the spirit of family and home. Piedmont Scout Tree Lot Online: it’s easy; it’s sustainable; it’s tradition; it’s relaxing; and it’s community. A limited option to purchase by phone will be available for customers who do not have online access. Trees and wreaths will be available for pickup or delivery after Thanksgiving. Home deliveries will be to customers’ front door. articles.text: Transitional Kindergarteners had their first day of school yesterday at Beach School on Tuesday, November 17. It may have been the second rainy day of the season, but the opening could not have come at a more fortuitous time. Alameda County was moved back into the purple tier of COVID restrictions this week, and only schools already in session are allowed to continue. If the TK class started one day later, it would have been a different story. A press release from Alameda County’s Department of Public Health states, “Any school that currently has students attending classes in person may continue to do so. Effective November 18 no additional schools may open for in-person instruction.” Piedmont School District’s painstaking and protracted plans to open in-person K-2 classes on December 1 and grades 3-5 on December 8 have been cancelled. California implemented Transitional Kindergarten in the fall of 2012. It is available only for students that turn five years old between September 2 and December 2. For the first week of class, parents are allowed to go onto campus with their TK students to help their transition to real school. After that, visitors on campus will be highly restricted. Students had an orientation on Monday, November 16, to see their new classroom and go over spacing and other COVID protocols. On Tuesday, Principal Michael Corritone personally welcomed parents and Piedmont’s youngest students. Most of the young scholars brought a small potted plant for their new teacher, Alexandra de Martini. TK students will have half-day classes Tuesday through Friday from 12:00 to 2:15 p.m., with distance learning on Mondays. Proud parents were on hand for their TK students’ first day of school. Millennium High School welcomed its freshmen back to campus on Friday, November 13, for 2 1/2 hours of advisory, tech support and supported study hall for the first time since March. Even with a surprise fire alarm and a quick trip outside, the return to campus was an overwhelming success. Students completed a health screener before arrival, wore masks, used hand sanitizer and sat in marked seats six feet apart with all the windows and doors open. With new safety precautions in place, students were still able to share stories with one another, joke and receive support from the staff on hand. “It was great to be here today,” exclaimed student Orla Cohen. Paraeducator Alisa Foster added, “I am so happy to be a part of this.” Students drew graphic representations of their identity and what was important to them as they introduced themselves to classmates they had met only on their computer screens. “Millennium is a small, tightknit community so it was really special to be able to welcome our new students to our campus,” said Principal Shannon Fierro. “I am so grateful to the staff and families and students for making this a safe, smooth and positive return,” she added. Additional small cohorts of MHS students, divided by grade, will be invited to campus over the next few weeks. One cohort of students will come to campus from 9:00 a.m.- 11:30 a.m. each Wednesday and Friday, through December 18. Students will have an hour of advisory and 75 minutes of supported study hall and instructional support. Each day of school in-person will have just one cohort on campus. Millennium will have 11 freshmen, 13 sophomores, 11 juniors and the 22 seniors (in two cohorts of 11). Students will leave campus at 11:30 a.m. and return home to complete the remainder of the school day (12:30 p.m. - 3:10 p.m.) remotely. Students on campus will be supervised by Principal Fierro with paraeducator support. Other teachers and support staff are invited and permitted to come and support but are not required to attend, student attendance is also optional. Prior to the return of Millennium students, only two small groups of Special Education students have been learning in-person. Separately, Piedmont schools welcomed back nine TK students yesterday at Beach School. Since Millennium was already in session prior to Alameda County moving into the purple tier, they are eligible to continue instruction. articles.text: Alameda County was moved into the purple – most restrictive – tier of COVID restrictions this week, meaning that elementary school classes in Piedmont will not open December 1 and 8 as planned. The school district is still working meet the requirements for reopening Details of its ongoing plans were discussed in the most recent School Board meeting, November 10. The Master Schedule for elementary schools has been finished, parents and students learned of their teacher assignments November 16. Secondary school teachers have completed the survey asking if they intend to teach in-person or remotely. articles.text: Here are some sensory tips and tricks If and when school returns masks will be required at all times on school grounds. As a parent, the thought of getting a young child to wear a mask brings up memories of my efforts to keep hats on my children in order to prevent sunburn. Strategies I tried included distracting them, finding hats with ties making it harder to pull off or I let them pick out their favorite team’s hat with its logo. It was a struggle, nevertheless. Similarly, wearing masks and/ or keeping them on for a prolonged period (over two hours) is sure to be challenging for most children. Here are some sensory-based tips and tricks for helping the resistive child. To begin, talk with your child. Be certain that they understand why they must wear a mask. There are many social stories for young children that address mask wearing. Next, acknowledge that wearing a mask is not easy and ask why they do not like wearing a mask. You will be surprised by their ability to pinpoint what is bothersome for them. With that, you can begin to find solutions to make mask wearing more tolerable. The most likely reason that children resist wearing a mask is that there are one or more sensory aspects that are bothersome. Think of a mask as a piece of clothing. We all know that fit and comfort can make or break your wearing a certain garment. How many of you are wearing fitted jeans as you work remotely? Some common reasons for mask avoidance include: • It feels rough or scratchy. • It tickles (too loose) or is too tight. • It smells inside. • It’s too hot and sweaty. • It hurts their ears. • It’s hard to breathe. Once you have a better understanding of which sensations make wearing a mask difficult, you are ready to find a more sensory-friendly mask for your child. First, consider the following. • Material – soft cotton, polyester/spandex • Shape - square or diamond • Strap style design - ear loops, single band with adjustable tug cord After you have settled on a mask that fits your child’s sensory needs, begin building their tolerance to wearing the mask. Have them wear the mask for short periods at home while engaged in fun activities. Gradually increase the time worn daily. As the wearing time lengthens, you may encounter new sensory obstacles such as ear pain, moisture issues or smells. Here are a few tricks for these issues: • Be sensitive to laundry detergent smells. Scent free or scented? • Consider a silicone mask bracket insert to reduce moisture and fogging glasses. • Button headbands for ear loop masks - no more tugging at ears. • Ear savers allow a mask to be attached behind the head instead of around the ears. • Disposable for lightweight choice. • Brush teeth prior to donning a mask. • Suck on a mint or hard candy. • Let your child pick out the mask with their favorite characters or color. Sometimes that is motivation enough. • Provide fidgets to keep hands busy to reduce the urge to touch or remove masks. Armed with these sensory tips and tricks, here’s to a successful transition back to in-person learning for our youngest students while wearing their sensory-friendly masks. articles.text: On a bright and chilly Sunday morning, November 8, car after car pulled up to deliver sweet treats through a backyard gate in central Piedmont. Behind the gate, a table held a delectable array of cakes, cookies, and tarts with a Halloween theme. The delicious dishes were made by students participating in the Top Chef Junior Piedmont competition, a student-led fundraiser for the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign. The fundraiser was created by Beach School 5th grader Luka Stevanovic. It was co-founded by 6th grader Preston Kwei, with organizing help from Piedmont High senior Bella Kjellen. The event raised $1,725 for the Giving Campaign and created a day of socially-distanced fun for young bakers and chefs across Piedmont. The Giving Campaign is a family affair for Stevanovic. “Part of why I did this is because of my aunt, Teebie Saunders. She is the head of the Giving Campaign,” he said. “I thought that this would be a way for people to raise money for the schools while having fun doing it.” Co-founder Preston Kwei had a similar motivation. “My parents have always supported the Giving Campaign, so I thought I should help in my own way too,” he added. The Kwei family hosted the socially-distanced judging portion of the competition in their backyard. The all-star panel of judges included chef Omri Aflalo of upcoming Oakland restaurant Town Revival; 4th grader Asher Dolid and his mother, Havens principal Anne Dolid; Beach teacher Claire Stephens; and middle school students Esme Krumins (6th grade), and Grace Rego (8th grade). Creating a cooking competition amid a global pandemic wasn’t easy, explained Rego. “The most challenging part was putting it together in a COVID world,” she said. “We made sure we were keeping safe distances and that the contestants were wearing masks when they dropped off their food.” On the morning of the event students met virtually via Zoom to review the rules, then began Luka Stevanovic (left), Preston Kwei, Esme Krummins, Grace Rego, and Bella Kjellen were the principal organizers of the successful Top Chef Junior event that raised over $1700 for the Giving Campaign. mixing, cooking, and baking in their own kitchens. At 12:30 p.m. they began delivering their creations for the judging. A total of 23 local students from 3rd to 8th grade participated. Krumins said the judging panel enjoyed their job. Reviewing all the entries turned out to be an arduous task. “I really liked tasting all the desserts! All of them were great,” she said. “At the end, we started to get really full. We had 23 things to taste, so I had to take very small bites.” The baking and cooking talent on display during the competition was impressive. Third grader Jane Weisner made pumpkin patch cake pops, painstakingly forming them with chopsticks. “I really like baking,” she said when dropping off her creation for the judges to sample. “The most fun was making the frosting!” Other creations included a cauldron filled with leaves and “Wild Mummy” jalapeño poppers wrapped in puff pastry created by 5th grader Cassidy Carter, and a massive “Apple Jack” cake shaped like a life-sized pumpkin, baked by Sophia and Callie Harris and Emma Sloan. The grand prize-winner was a chocolate cake baked by 3rd grader Elizabeth Payne with intricate fondant decorations. Judge and professional chef Aflalo was particularly impressed by the fondant bats attached to wires that appeared to float above the cake. Tied for second place were 5th grader Bailey Ramillosa (vegan chocolate cupcakes with cookie tombstones), and 3rd grader Ariana Bennett (gluten-free black-bottom pumpkin cupcakes with ghost cream cheese frosting and chocolate spider webs). Honorable mention awards went to 5th grader Lucy Dorsey (pumpkin-spice doughnuts encased in a chocolate shell), and 4th grader Annabelle Allessio (meatloaf zombie head emerging from a pool of tomato sauce “blood” with claws of pizza crust). Stevanovic and Kwei said they were very pleased with the results of their hard work. “We are so proud of our amazing turnout. We can’t wait to do another round,” said Stevanovic. Student judge Asher Dolid hopes to see the Piedmont Top Chef Junior competition become an annual event for the Giving Campaign. “I want people to know that this event is helping the Piedmont schools,” he said. “It’s supporting other people in a way that builds the community.”

articles.text: A time of year to remember to shop locally Piedmont Avenue businesses that have struggled to stay in business will soon see relief with all stores being open during the holiday season. Due to the COVID epidemic, there won’t be a Holiday Stroll, or the traditional tree lighting ceremony at Key Route Plaza on Piedmont Avenue & 41st Street. “We are not doing the tree lighting this year,” confirmed retailer Philippa Roberts. “It takes a lot of time and money, neither of which is very abundant these days.” Businesses desperately need a strong holiday season this year. Most have had to be creative to save their businesses. Claudio Luporini, owner of Bella Ceramica and a personal friend of Kris Kringle, said that Santa will have to skip his annual trip to the Avenue due to the coronavirus health restrictions in place. However, Luporini as always, will provide egg nog, hot totties, hot cocoa, bubbly, and cookies for customers. Nathan Walden, owner of Nathan & Co. with locations on Piedmont Ave. and College Ave., has been busy adapting to the times. For Black Friday – the Friday after Thanksgiving – and the following week, if customers say they are friends of Oakland Tech High School or Claremont Middle School, 20 percent of the sale will go to the Teacher’s Association for that school. Nathan and Co. was quick to jump on a new platform called www.KeepOaklandAlive.com. The website has teamed up with the most popular stores in Oakland by offering free two-day delivery. The fabric of the community lies at stake this holiday season, local business have ramped up their online and curbside pickup options to do what they can to keep people engaged and safe. “Rest assured, Piedmont Avenue is open and ready for business,” said longtime Piedmont Ave. volunteer Ronile Lahti. “Our holiday shopping message is Shop Local, Shop Oakland, but Shop Piedmont Avenue first. If we don’t have it, we’ll do our best to find it for you.” – Ronile Lahti Piedmont Ave. volunteer “The whole year has been just a huge challenge. We are concentrating on PR and pushing our website. I have brought back a publicist to help drive traffic to the website to bring in some dollars, but business is still down 50 percent.” Walden has kept his commitments to the community however.

As reported last week, Piedmont High’s football program is not the only sport at the school getting its offseason conditioning programs underway. From 3 pm through 9:30 p.m. athletes of multiple sports can be spotted with conditioning programs. Returning to Witter Field for training last week were the football team, water polo team for dry land conditioning, cross-country teams, volleyball team, boys’ and girls’ lacrosse teams, boys’ basketball and baseball teams, and the girls’ softball team. “This week has been very busy, but everyone is excited. Just being at school is a terrific change for these student-athletes. You can tell the kids and coaches are ecstatic to see each other,” he said. However, the California Interscholastic Federation, the governing body for high school sports, announced this Monday, November 16 that competition between schools is still not allowed “until new guidance is provided,” meaning the state must still pass through health measures before allowing interscholastic matches. “In today’s COVID-19 press Staff Photos briefing, Governor Newsom and Dr. Mark Ghaly from the California Department of Public Health disclosed that the release of updated youth sports guidance has been postponed. Therefore, the current guidance remains in effect, and CIF competitions are not allowed until new guidance is provided,” wrote the CIF in a media release. So what does practicing for sports mean without the gear required to play the sport? In short, a whole bunch of running. “We’re getting in shape. We’re running routes, and a lot of sprints. Piedmont High School athletics recently resumed on a limited basis, and Witter Field is reserved for these programs each weekday from 3:00 to 9:00 pm. The Windsor Avenue gate, Wildwood Elementary School playground, baseball and softball fields, batting cages, and Witter Field House restrooms remain closed. Individuals must wear face coverings, maintain at least sixfoot social distancing from others who are not part of the same household or living unit, and avoid all social interaction when sick with a fever, cough, or other COVID-19 symptoms. The District previously closed Witter Field due to widespread and persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County order at the Field. articles.text: Cal steamrolled in opener vs. UCLA; Stanford fails by 3 to Colorado Photos courtesy of Mercury News Cal struggled in its short-notice season-opener against UCLA in a 34-10 loss. The University of California Golden Bears finally got their season started, but it didn’t go their way in a devastating 34-10 loss to the UCLA Bruins on Sunday morning, November 15. Stanford, meanwhile, fell short of a fourth quarter comeback in a nail-biting 35-32 loss to Colorado on Saturday. The Bears’ game against UCLA came on short notice after originally scheduling a game with with Arizona State. However, the Sun Devils’ program has had an outbreak of COVID-19, including head coach Herm Edwards, and had to cancel. Cal’s season opener against Washington on November 7 was wiped out due to COVID protocols that ravaged the Bears’ defensive line. On Friday, the Pac 12 announced that California agreed to play UCLA on 9 a.m. on Sunday after the Bruins’ game against Utah was canceled after a Utes’ virus outbreak as well. Are you following this so far? This is the new normal. Cal’s lack of training showed, notably on the lack of tackling by the defense. The Golden Bears missed a plethora of tackles in Sunday’s game, many of which led to first downs and big breaks. The offense, meanwhile, showed the same inconsistencies which plagued them in previous years. Quarterback Chase Garbers was everywhere with the ball, going 18 of 33 for 122 yards and an interception. His offensive line didn’t do Cal any favors, allowing five sacks and nine tackles for loss. “We haven’t played a football game in about a year. We haven’t played anyone but ourselves in a real, live game scenario, live tempo, tackling, everything, in about a year. So there are obviously going to be some hurdles there,” Garbers said, via the Associated Press. “On both sides of the ball, we didn’t play to what we expected to and first game in a COVID season, some of those hurdles are expected.” Cal looks ahead to Oregon State this Saturday, November 21. Oregon State is 0-2 after losing 38-28 to Washington State in Week 1 and nearly pulling off an upset in a loss to Washington, 27-21. The Beavers just held the Huskies to 141 passing yards, and given Cal’s struggles against the Bruins, it’s conceivable that the Bears will try to get the running game going early with Christopher Brown. Stanford Stanford fell short of a comeback victory after trailing the Buffs 35-16 in the fourth quarter. Quarterback Davis Mills was a standout in his first appearance this season, going 31 of 56 for 327 yards with one passing and rushing touchdown. The Cardinal forced three punts in the final quarter, scoring their final touchdown with 2:34 remaining but retaining the ball for the last possession with just 10 seconds on the clock. Stanford plays Washington State this weekend, and it could be an offensive battle given that the Cougars are allowing 516 yards per game but are averaging 430 offensive yards. Mills is liekly to be the focus again, especially when factoring in the struggles of the Cardinal running game, which is averaging only 3.3 yards per carry. Look for Mills and the passing attack to open early, then begin to mix the attack with runs. It will be an interesting game to watch for both Cal and stanforrd, which wil meet one another in the histroic Big Game on Friday, November 27, the day afer Thanksgiving. articles.text: 6-2 win over Panama; 0-0 draw with Wales Join the bandwagon now before 2022 and the inevitable U.S. soccer craze in 2026. The United State Men’s National Team is putting its roster together for the 2022 World Cup, and doing so with a collective average age of 21 in the two recent friendlies with Wales on Thursday, November 12, and Panama on Monday, November 16. They drew 0-0 with the Welsh and dominated 6-2 over the Panamanians. Impressively, Nov. 12 was the team’s first match since February. The team had a roster with 22 of the 23 players from foreign clubs. Prior to the match, manager Gregg Berhalter said he’s hoping to show fans signs of hope for the future. It’s fair to say he’s doing just that. To put into context, Berhalter featured players who –theoretically – could appear on the men’s team for the next 10 years. The squad showed a swagger that is unalike the U.S. men’s program. They featured overlapping runs, balls over the top from the back, and symmetry one wouldn’t expect from a team that, largely, was playing together for the very first time. When realizing that they’ve had limited training together due to COVID-19, their two friendlies were that more impressive. Although the boys conceded a goal against Panama in the eighth minute, they resoundingly responded with the equalizer by 18-year old Gio Reyna after the young star from Dortmund smashed in a free kick from a yard above the penalty area. He’s starting in the 10-role, Central Attacking Midfield, and schematically rotated to both sides of the pitch at times. Soon after, 20-year old Nicholas Gioacchini rebounded home his first goal for the U.S. team in the 18th after Uly Llanez, 19-years old, shot a hard ball on net that skipped off the keeper and conveniently to Gioacchini’s feet. Photo courtesy of MLS.com 17-year old Yunus Musah became the first U.S. Men’s National Team player under age 18 to start two matches. Four minutes later, Giocchini scored again, heading in perhaps the most beautifully worked USMNT goal in recent years. It started with a Tyler Adams (21- years old), sending a ball in to Weston McKennie, who lobbed a pass off the touchline to center back Matt Miazga, heading a pass to Giochinni for the goal. But Panama drew closer at 3-2 when Jose Fajardo scored his second in the 79th, but USMNT responded with quickness once again. A pair of 20-year olds from clubs in the Netherlands, Sebastian Soto headed home a perfect cross from Richie Ledezma—both were making their first U.S. appearances, for a 4-2 lead in the 83rd. Sebastian Lletget, the only MLS player on the roster, scored the fifth with another nice header on a pass fullback Reggie Cannon in 87th. Ledezma got his second assist on a long cross to Soto in the 91st. Scorelsss vs. Wales As for their 0-0 draw with the Welsh, it was somewhat a victory for U.S. fans and pundits from the standpoint of sheer potential . Sergino Dest was dynamic. The 19-year old Barcelona rising star danced on the ball with the grace one would expect from a Barca fullback. Meanwhile, 17-year old Yunus Musah of Velencia became the first player under 18-years old to start in two U.S. matches. Of the current 23-man roster, Tim Ream is the oldest at 33, and starting centerback John Brooks is next oldest at 27. The roster currently includes six players still in their teens The United States has no matches scheduled for the remainder of the year. The next International break for European clubs is for March 27, which coincides with CONCACAF’s World Cup qualifying matches.

articles.text: French composer Camille Saiant-Saens. There are many famous pieces of music which everyone knows. But not everyone knows from whence they came. Here are some of the stories that nobody knows due to ghost writers behind the fame. Everybody knows Carnival of the Animals by French composer Saint-Saens. It is his most famous piece. But it is not original. As you will see, excepting for Einstein’s famous theory, nothing comes out of the blue. Carnival was so popular that Saint-Saens forbade publication except for “The Swan“. But his idea for Carnival was not exactly original. Nine years before he wrote it, a friend named Hubert Leonard composed “Five Humerus Pieces”. History and the public has long forgotten Leonard’s work. But Saint-Saens reaped fame and fortune. Niccolo Paganini is considered the most famous violinist of all time. His fourth violin Concerto wowed Paris in the 1830s. It is a dramatic showpiece displaying incredible virtuosity. But its opening salvo is entirely derived from a student concerto by Vivaldi. The important German-American conductor and educator Walter Damrosch wrote a popular song entitled “Danny Deaver”. The song gives every hint of genius. But there has never been a mention that Damrosch drew as his inspiration a funeral march from a Beethoven piano Sonata. One of the greatest violin sonatas was written by the Belgian composer Caesar Franck. But cellists insist that Franck conceived the work as a cello piece. This, may I say, is absolutely incorrect. Franck wrote his great sonata as a wedding present for violinist Eugene Ysaye in 1886. But the impetus for his monumental work actually derives from a sonata by a friend of Franck, the Hungarian violinist Hubay. He wrote his sonata in 1871, a full 15 years before Franck wrote his sonata. Sometimes fate goes the other way. Sometimes composers write music which is assumed to be folk music. Dvorak’s New World Symphony acquired folk music status when it became the popular song, “Goin’ home.” The great American songwriter Stephen Foster contributed a host of songs which suffered the same fate. History can often be selective. How often does the public celebrate the works of composers like Saint-Saens, Paganini, Beethoven, and Franck? Lost in the shuffle is their inspiration. So when you listen to Carnival of the Animals, or Paganini’s 4th Violin Concerto, or the Franck Sonata, please give a thought to those “other composers” who received no credit - the ghost writers. A holiday recipe The case of the vanishing duck Duck is a festive dish, especially when the weather turns cold. The one I made was special, and it vanished before I could take its picture. Preparation is easy, despite numerous ingredients. Preheat the oven to 450°. Take a large skillet and put some oil in it; brown the duck lightly. Be sure to prick the skin in a few places. Place the duck in a covered roasting pan, add salt and pepper, and squeeze three or four tangerines over the duck. Add the rind along with two minced trumpet mushrooms, one onion and two cloves of garlic. Around the duck scatter some of your favorite dried fruit. I use cranberries and apricots, but you can add any fruit you want including a fresh apple or guava. To keep the duck moist, pour at least 3 tablespoons of wine vinegar over the duck. By Joseph Gold There are many famous pieces of music which everyone knows. But not everyone knows from whence they came. Here are some of the stories that nobody knows due to ghost writers behind the fame. Everybody knows Carnival of the Animals by French composer Saint-Saens. It is his most famous piece. But it is not original. As you will see, excepting for Einstein’s famous theory, nothing comes out of the blue. Carnival was so popular that Saint-Saens forbade publication except for “The Swan“. But his idea for Carnival was not exactly original. Nine years before he wrote it, a friend named Hubert Leonard composed “Five Humerus Pieces”. History and the public has long forgotten Leonard’s work. But Saint-Saens reaped fame and fortune. Niccolo Paganini is considered the most famous violinist of all time. His fourth violin Concerto wowed Paris in the 1830s. It is a dramatic showpiece displaying incredible virtuosity. But its opening salvo is entirely derived from a student concerto by Vivaldi. The important German-American conductor and educator Walter Damrosch wrote a popular song entitled “Danny Deaver”. The song gives every hint of genius. But there has never been a mention that Damrosch drew as his inspiration a funeral march from a Beethoven piano Sonata. One of the greatest violin sonatas was written by the Belgian composer Caesar Franck. But cellists insist that Franck conceived the work as a cello piece. This, may I say, is absolutely incorrect. Franck wrote his great sonata as a wedding present for violinist Eugene Ysaye in 1886. But the impetus for his monumental work actually derives from a sonata by a friend of Franck, the Hungarian violinist Hubay. He wrote his sonata in 1871, a full 15 years before Franck wrote his sonata. Sometimes fate goes the other way. Sometimes composers write music which is assumed to be folk music. Dvorak’s New World Symphony acquired folk music status when it became the popular song, “Goin’ home.” The great American songwriter Stephen Foster contributed a host of songs which suffered the same fate. History can often be selective. How often does the public celebrate the works of composers like Saint-Saens, Paganini, Beethoven, and Franck? Lost in the shuffle is their inspiration. So when you listen to Carnival of the Animals, or Paganini’s 4th Violin Concerto, or the Franck Sonata, please give a thought to those “other composers” who received no credit - the ghost writers. articles.text: Richard Gere and Hilary Swank in Amelia. Movie review by Chris Honoré Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific Ocean on July 2, 1937. She was attempting to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, something that had never been done before. Her success depended not only on her flying skills but on the ability of Fred Noonan, her navigator. On the Pacific leg of the flight, he would have to find a mere speck of land, Howland Island, in a body of water so vast that there would be no second chance. Told that it was dangerous, perhaps reckless in the extreme – there was a good Hilary Swank as Amelia Earhart in Amelia. chance she would run out of fuel – Earhart was committed to trying. She left Miami on June 1 and began what would be her final journey. Earhart was driven to fly, consumed with an unrelenting passion to be in the air, no matter the craft no matter the challenge. She broke records, flew solo across the Atlantic in a gorgeous, red Lockeed Vega 58, landing to her delight and surprise in Ireland. Her passion for flight was unequivocal. What the film is unable to do is capture that bright, burning need to be aloft. Had the movie focused on flight, her desire since childhood to pilot airplanes, and explored the serenity she found aloft with the discomfort she found on land, then this would have been an examination of her as a person and not just a quickly glimpse into the life of this highly commercialized heroine. Hillary Swank, portraying Earhart, is a dead ringer for the fresh-faced, tossle-hair, androgynous flier. But for reasons known only to the screenwriters, Swank, an accomplished Oscar-winning actress, is never asked to stretch in the role. Earhart was controversial, she was self-absorbed, single-minded and independent in a time when women were more typically seen and not heard. In the years leading up to World War II, most women were still home. The war changed everything and women in pants and leather jackets, building airplanes and then flying them, become far more common. Amelia misses a wonderful opportunity to say something interesting about this woman who was so adored, so famous, whose disappearance, without a trace remains, some 70 years later, a subject of intense fascination. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Cat Returns Movie review by Chris Honoré The Cat Returns, directed by Hiroyuki Murita (his only feature for Studio Ghibli), is based on a manga story written by Aoi Hiragi. The narrative has at its center Haru (Anne Hathaway), a shy, insecure Tokyo schoolgirl who has a repressed affinity for cats (she can talk to them). One day, when she is out and about, she saves a cat from being run over by a truck. As it turns out, the cat, called Lune (Andrew Bevis), is the son of the Cat King (Tim Curry). Wanting to reward Haru’s heroism, the King insists that she come to the Cat Kingdom and there he creates a plan to have Haru marry Lune. But in order for this to take place, Haru must begin her transformation into a cat. Soon Haru grows ears, whiskers and a tail. Distressed by what is happening, she realizes that she must escape the Cat Kingdom before it is too late for her to be able to return to her human world. It’s at this point in the story that the story drops down an Alice in Wonderland rabbit hole and becomes a mix of characters and silly plans focused on Haru finding a portal that will return her to her previous life. She hears a soft feminine voice telling her to find a chunky cat named Muta (Peter Boyle). Muta leads her to the Baron (Gary Elwes), a statuette brought to life with the help of Toto (Elliot Gould), a stone raven. And so on. They plan and connive to rescue Haru, all while trying to avoid the King. When Lune discovers Haru’s wish to escape, he reveals he wants to marry another, Yuki (Judy Greer), a servant working in the kingdom. I would judge that The Cat Returns is best suited for young viewers. Unlike the work produced by Studio Ghibli, its story is slight, definitely cartoony, and just hectic fun. However, the quality of the animation, as always, is superb with a strong color palette with a cast of characters that will engage. The Cat Returns (2002). Directed by Hiroyuki Murita. Animé by Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Anne Hathaway, Gary Elwes, Peter Boyle and Elliot Gould. 1 hr., 15 min. Rated G.

articles.text: On a chilly Friday morning, October 30th, about 20 dogs of all sizes and furs celebrated Halloween by dressing up in costumes and trick-or-treating under the redwoods in Dracena Park. Heidi Kistler, owner of Positively Pampered Pets invited her Piedmont clients to join her on a wild romp as costumed dogs celebrated Howl-O-Ween, while nearby small children giggled as they watched from the play structure. It was the first year the dogs had their costume party away from Bushy Dell Creek, the traditional meeting and sniffing Hazel the Golden Retriever wore a lovely Snow White ensemble, and the small but mighty 15-pound Agnes, a black pug, was transformed into a healthy Pug Taco. Woody from Toy Story was there, as well as a ladybug, an ostrich and a sizeable muscle man hound that appeared determined to sniff all canines and humans. Many girl dogs wore beautiful gowns imitating the Disney Princesses, while the boy dogs seemed to favor various Premier League soccer stars. Amazingly, nary a dog growl was heard. articles.text: Walking through town it is impossible not to notice the aesthetic impact of different ancillary structures that are an integral part of the design of many homes. Falling somewhere between architecture and landscape architecture, fences, walls, and their associated gates are chief among these. They can enhance (or unfortunately sometimes compromise) the building, landscape and/or site design. So…what constitutes nice retaining walls, appealing fences or beautiful gates? Like all of the discussions in this column, I point out different ideas or considerations that hopefully help to answer this ongoing question. But there are usually many good answers as well as exceptions to every general rule. What is ultimately important is just what looks and feels right – what appeals to us. That being said, here are some thoughts. The first thing that comes to mind is that these secondary structures need as much study and consideration as the main building(s) or landscape treatment of which they are a part. It is unfortunately obvious when they are designed as simply an afterthought. Fences, walls and gates certainly must be in the same architectural “family” as the home, though this doesn’t mean they have to be exactly the same form, color or even the same material. They do need to relate most appropriately. They are indeed an opportunity to aesthetically deviate to some degree and add interest to both the building(s) and property. Fences or walls can be used to provide privacy, add security, or merely to demarcate the edge of private or semi-private spaces between adjacent properties, or between a property and the street. After adherence to the architectural style of the buildings, the intended use or function of the barrier will be the primary consideration in determining its type, shape and character, i.e., solid (wall) vs, airy (spaced boards), height, extent, and access or gate placements. Gates are, of course, a promPhotos and sketch by Will Adams Photos above and below: Two well designed variations of the traditional white picket fence, both stepping to nicely accommodate the slope of the sidewalk and site, as well as adding interest and texture to the street.

articles.text: SUNROOM BEDROOM WIC LIVING ROOM KITCHEN BATH DINING LAUNDRY GARAGE GARAGE WIC BEDROOM BEDROOM FOYER BEDROOM PORCH Many older adults prefer living in their homes as long as possible in order to maintain their daily lifestyle in a familiar environment. However, aging typically brings challenges with it, including reduced vision and hearing, decreased mobility, and the increased risk of falls. Here are some practical and easy design solutions to consider to make your home safer and easier to live in as you age. Foyers Install an outdoor motion light sensor to ensure good visibility when unlocking your door and trying to find the light switch in the foyer. When it comes to door handles, lever type handles are easier to grip and operate than door knobs. Make sure your entry foyer is free of obstructions and well-lit as well. Living Rooms Finishes and layout of living areas have a big impact on a person’s ability to move around safely and be independent. Make sure you have a clear path with no clutter when moving from one room to another. Transitions between different floor finishes should be smooth to prevent falls. If you have area rugs, make sure to install non-slip pads or double-sided carpet tape to reduce the risk of tripping. Short pile carpets are safer than large loop carpets as they help increase mobility. Kitchens Kitchens are typically one of the busiest rooms in our homes. Drawers and pull out base cabinets are much easier to use than cabinet doors and fixed shelves. If you do not have the budget to replace existing cabinet doors you can simply add roll out trays or a lazy susan inside the cabinets. Another easy retrofit is to replace cabinet door knobs with curved edge handles that have enough surface area for an easy grasp. Be careful not to choose handles with sharp edges that can snag clothes or be painful to bump into. Also, lever style faucets are much easier to operate than faucets with turn handles. Bathrooms Most falls happen in the bathroom, so special attention should be paid to safety in your bathrooms. Nightlights are extremely helpful to locate a bathroom easily in the middle of the night. Grab bars are life savers in many situations. Common areas for grab bars are inside your showers or tubs and adjacent to the toilet for ease of mobility and safety. Towel bars may not support your weight, so they are not safe to rely on as a grab bar. Consider adding textured strips on the bottom of your tub or shower to prevent slips and falls while bathing. Similarly, secure your bath mats with nonslip pads or choose non-slip mats. Bedrooms As we age, our eyes lose the ability to differentiate between shades of colors. Use light switch covers that contrast with wall colors so they are easy to see. Choose solid colored low pile carpet for your bedrooms in lieu of patterned carpet that may be confusing and distracting as aging brings declining vision. Laundry areas Raising your washer and dryer off the floor makes it easier to load and unload without bending for long periods. General It is essential to have a welllit house with a consistent level of ambient lighting. Make sure stairways are well-lit and have handrails at least on one side. Replacing toggle style light switches with lever style switches will make the operation easier and faster. These simple upgrades will increase your quality of life and help you enjoy your home for many years to come. Yildiz Duransoy is Project Manager at BDE Architecture in San Francisco and is a member of the Piedmont Planning Commission. For information, contact yduransoy@gmail.com.

articles.text: Roland Marzolf (left) and brother Wayne, founders of Drawbridge Cellars. In 2008, Piedmont resident Wayne Marzolf teamed up with his brother Roland for a little experiment: let’s try to make a couple of barrels of wine in the garage. The Malbec wine – all 50 cases of it – was a huge hit. Not being bonded, he gave it away to friends and family. (Full disclosure. I am a longtime friend of Wayne and Roland.) “I really didn’t know what I was doing,” Wayne said later. “I just threw the grapes and yeast in the barrel and hoped for the best. Beginners luck I guess.” Over the ensuing years Wayne and Roland, who ran a successful East Bay construction company, began to ramp up their wine production. They opened up a makeshift winery in the Oakland building that housed their construction offices. Over the years they bought more and more barrels and acquired more equipment. In 2017 the winery was bonded and production rose to 350 cases. They both have retired from the construction business, and now the winery takes up most of their time. They named the winery Drawbridge in honor of its home, the city of Alameda which is an island serviced by multiple drawbridges. Today Drawbridge Cellars produces 10 different bottlings with an emphasis on Rhone varietals. They source from many different varied vineyards around the state, sometimes even picking the grapes themselves. As a friend, I have had a ringside seat watching the wines and the winery grow and improve. Wayne and Roland have gone from a couple of guys with good luck to skilled winemakers whose chemical and technical skills have improved greatly. What I like about their wines is that they still feel homemade and down to earth, not commercially manipulated like so many modern California wines. The wines are just beginning to be available in the East Bay. You can find them at Mulberry’s Market in Piedmont and a few restaurants in Alameda. But the best thing to do is call Wayne and Roland and make an appointment to meet at the winery tasting room in Oakland. They are happy to pour their current releases and even better, there is no tasting fee. Drawbridge Cellars wine label.

articles.text: Like it or not, it looks like we’ll be celebrating this holiday season mostly at home, shelving our plans for festive meals and parties out in favor of more cooking and eating in. Even more than usual, this means our choices about what we eat and how we prepare it matters more than ever. Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan and yearly greenhouse gas inventories tell us that our homes and cars create the bulk of our collective emissions within the boundaries of our fair town. But you might be surprised to learn that the impact of our food choices dwarfs that of our energy usage in the grand scheme of things. “Plant-rich diets,” which basically means eating less red meat and dairy, pencils out as one of the biggest solutions according to Project Drawdown, a group that models the point when levels of greenhouse gases stop climbing and start to steadily decline. A study this month in Science magazine concludes that we cannot possibly reach urgent climate goals, in the US or globally, without reforming how we eat and the way we farm. The real biggie is food waste According to multiple sources, 30-40% of food goes to waste, which means land and resources used and greenhouse gases emitted in producing it were unnecessary. On top of that, food we discard into the trash (rather than our green compost bins) creates methane, a greenhouse gas much more potent than carbon dioxide, as it decomposes in landfills. Stop and think about that: we don’t eat 30-40% of the food we grow, process, distribute and buy! We’ve all had the experience of finding wilted produce in our crisper and “vintage” leftovers on a forgotten shelf. But with some vigilance and motivation, it’s possible to battle food waste in our homes. I’m a fan of using grocery delivery services (Good Eggs is my favorite) to schedule multiple deliveries per week and avoid overbuying. It can also help to master a few dishes like frittatas, soups, stir fries, and fried rice, that readily accept bits of leftover vegetables or meats. And definitely compost rather than trashing food scraps, but try not to let compost be an excuse to waste food. Reducing food waste is the single most impactful Drawdown solution, with a much bigger impact than solar or electric cars. But, when it comes to reversing climate change, we don’t have the luxury of either/or solutions. We need to eat down the food chain, and reduce food waste, and add solar, and switch to electric cars – and do it all soon. StopWaste and the NRDC’s Save the Food campaign provide a range of practical tips and tools, like food storage reference guides and meal-planning “guestimators” that help you to buy and serve accurate quantities. So, let’s make the most of this mostly at-home holiday season to cultivate some planet-friendly food practices, and carry them with us post-pandemic and beyond. Susan Miller-Davis is a member of Piedmont Connect.
articles.title: Recipe for climate action at the holiday table

articles.text: The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held on December 4 but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,” she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to-go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.
articles.title: Cancer League Holly Ball to be virtual on December 4

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: It is with great sorrow that we inform all of you that our dear Mother, Alpha Mae Beamer, passed away on October 13, 2020. articles.text: Piedmont Shell Auto Care at Grand & Wildwood Avenues. Piedmont Shell Auto Care, located at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenue, has been granted a conditional use permit by the city to operate a retail store on its property. Owner Jeff Hansen stated in a request to the city on October 9 that he would like to add a convenience store element to the gas and auto repair shop. Hansen stated that the addition “will create a full gas station experience” for customers. On November 9, the Planning Commission unanimously recommended the approval of a conditional use permit. The application reviewed by City Council on November 16 proposed to add a commercial retail component to the existing facility. The Planning Commission’s recommendation stated that the retail store is primarily intended to serve Piedmont residents, in that Piedmont residents make up the majority of customers of the gas station. The commission also found that an added retail component will not have a material, adverse effect on the health, safety, or welfare of residents. Considerations for the finding include no substantial increase in traffic, parking needs or noise. Minimal interior changes will include the addition of shelves and refrigeration, according to the application. The anticipated annual revenue could be as much as $100,000.

articles.text: Captain Cal and his adopted sisters have found a permanent home at the zoo in Columbus, Ohio. The three orphaned mountain lion cubs, all rescued from the destructive Zogg and August Complex fires, will be traveling together on a flight to Ohio in the coming weeks. Cal Fire Firefighters spotted Captain Cal limping down a burned-out road in Redding on September 30. The severely burned cub’s future seemed grim; Cal required surgery, antibiotics, supportive fluids, pain medication, daily bandage changes, and round-the-clock care. He was only 3.75 pounds when he arrived at the Oakland Zoo’s Vet Hospital. Director of Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, Dr. Alex Herman, along with her staff and an expert wound specialist from UC Davis Veterinary Medicine Teaching Hospital, performed extensive surgery to remove the pads of his burnt paws so they could be allowed to regrow and heal. Columbus Zoo staff expressed their desire to eventually introduce the three cubs to their female mountain lion, Jessie. Jessie is 17 years old and has surpassed the median life expectancy of 16 years for mountain lions in human care. She is now nearly blind, but in overall good health, and the Columbus Zoo team notes that she has a sweet disposition with other mountain lions. Jessie and her brother, Billy were both rescued from a wildfire in 2004.
